Sometimes the lectures are too theoretical, and it's hard to connect the concepts to real-world problem solving. There is also a lack of consistent high-quality learning materials that support practical application.

(Good Experience) In my programming course, we had a project where we had to build a small application to solve a real problem, like a to-do list manager. The hands-on nature of it, where I had to figure out the logic and debug my own code, was incredibly effective. It was challenging but satisfying to see the final product work. This is a great example of problem-solving in action
The physical study environment is quiet and conducive to focused work, which is good for when I need to concentrate on coding without distractions.

The main challenge is that the library's physical collection is almost entirely irrelevant to my field. As a Full Stack Developer, I don't need physical textbooks because technology changes too fast books are often outdated by the time they are published. The library's value for me would be in digital resources, but that's where the problems are.

(Bad Experience) I once went to the library hoping to find resources on a specific, modern JavaScript framework I was learning for a project. The few books they had on web development were years old, covering outdated technologies. It was a complete waste of time. I ended up using my mobile data to search for online documentation and tutorials, which I could have done from home.
When the online portal works properly, it is convenient to register for classes and check my grades from anywhere without having to wait in line

The biggest challenge is system reliability. During peak times (like the start of registration), the portal often crashes or becomes extremely slow. Additionally, the information about course prerequisites and waitlists is sometimes unclear or changes unexpectedly.

(Bad Experience) Last semester, on registration day, the system kept timing out right when I tried to submit my course selections. By the time I could finally get back in, the advanced programming class I needed (which is only offered once a year) was full. I had to scramble to find alternatives and ended up falling behind in my graduation plan. It was frustrating because the issue wasn't my preparation, but the unreliable technology.
It's conveniently located on campus, so I can grab a quick meal between classes without having to leave and waste time. It's also a good place to meet up with classmates to discuss projects.

The main challenges are the long waiting times during peak hours and the lack of healthy, nutritious food options. Most of the food is fried, heavy, or repetitive, which affects my energy and concentration for afternoon coding sessions.

When I did stay there, the proximity to campus was the biggest advantage. I could wake up later and still make it to class on time, and it was easy to access the library and lab facilities late at night when I was working on projects

The main challenges were the unreliable internet connection and the slow response to maintenance requests. As a developer, I need stable internet to work on my projects, and it was frustrating when issues like a broken desk lamp or a leaking tap took weeks to get fixed.

(Bad Experience) During my second year, I had a major group project deadline. My room's Wi-Fi router was malfunctioning, and I couldn't connect to my online repositories or documentation. I reported it immediately, but it took the maintenance team almost two weeks to come and fix it. I had to rely on my mobile hotspot for days, which was slow and used up all my data. It was incredibly stressful and made collaborating with my team much harder than it needed to be.

Courses are most engaging when there   is a real interaction, like open discussions where students can question ideas, share perspectives, and connect theory to real-life situations. Practical sessions also make a big difference because they turn abstract concepts into something you can actually apply and understand. I also value when instructors encourage participation and create space for different viewpoints. It makes the learning environment more collaborative and helps the material stick better than just listening to lectures alone.

Some of the main challenges I have experienced include:
Too much focus on one-way lectures with limited interaction or discussion
Difficulty connecting theoretical content to practical, real-world application
Limited time for questions or deeper explanation during class
Uneven pace, where some topics move too fast while others feel slow
Lack of sufficient practical sessions or hands-on activities
Minimal feedback on assignments or participation
These issues can sometimes make it harder to stay fully engaged or to clearly understand how to apply what is being taught.

In one course, we had a session where the instructor moved beyond the usual lecture and gave us a real-world case to work on in small groups.
Instead of just explaining the theory, we had to apply the concepts to solve a practical problem and then present our approach to the class. The discussion that followed was open and interactive, with different groups defending their ideas and the instructor guiding us with questions rather than giving direct answers.
That experience stood out because it made the material easier to understand and remember. It also built confidence in using what we learned, not just memorizing it for exams. It felt like genuine learning rather than just completing a requirement.
